questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit have jurisdiction over a TTAB opposition appeal instead of the district court?
questions.question_body: I'm reading Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., and the court says it has jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(4)(B) to review a Trademark Trial and Appeal Board decision. I thought trademark disputes typically go to federal district court. Can someone explain why TTAB opposition decisions are appealed directly to the Federal Circuit rather than a district court, and what types of TTAB decisions fall under this jurisdictional statute?

questions.title: Does the TTAB need to analyze all 13 DuPont factors in a likelihood-of-confusion determination?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., the court quotes M2 Software for the proposition that the Board need not consider every DuPont factor, only those 'that are relevant and of record.' But the opinion also says likelihood of confusion is a question of law based on underlying factual findings under the DuPont factors. If the Board can skip factors, how does an appellant know which factors will be considered? And does the Board have an obligation to explain why certain factors are irrelevant, or can it just silently omit them? In this case, the court only discusses factors 1, 2, and 6—does that mean the Board only considered those three, or did it consider others that weren't challenged on appeal?

questions.title: What does 'legally identical, in part' mean in the DuPont factor analysis for similarity of services?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., the Board found that Apex's 'banking and financing services' and CC Serve's 'credit card services' are 'legally identical, in part' because dictionary definitions of 'banking' and 'finance' encompass extending credit through credit cards. I'm confused about what 'legally identical, in part' means as a legal standard. Does it mean the services overlap but aren't fully identical? And how does this relate to the test from Coach Services that products need only be 'related in some manner'? Is 'legally identical' a higher degree of similarity than 'related,' and does it automatically trigger a finding that the factor weighs in favor of confusion, or is it just one piece of evidence?

questions.title: Why was it inconsistent for the TTAB to use different standards of 'similarity' under DuPont factors 2 and 6?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., the Federal Circuit vacated the Board's sixth DuPont factor analysis because the Board narrowed the universe of third-party marks to only those for 'credit card services,' excluding marks for other banking and financing services. The court said this was inconsistent with the Board's second factor analysis, where it found the parties' services to be 'highly similar' and even 'legally identical, in part.' I understand the court's reasoning that the Board shouldn't apply a stricter similarity standard under factor 6 than under factor 2, but is the court saying the Board MUST use the exact same scope of similarity across all factors? Aren't the factors asking different questions—factor 2 is about the parties' own services, while factor 6 is about third-party marks on similar goods? Could there be a legitimate reason to define 'similar' differently in each context?

questions.title: How does the sixth DuPont factor (third-party marks) affect the first DuPont factor (commercial impression)?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., the court remanded the first DuPont factor analysis solely because reconsideration of the sixth factor 'may result in a different determination of the mark's commercial strength or weakness and affect the overall commercial impression.' I don't understand the doctrinal link between these two factors. The first factor is about similarity of the marks themselves (appearance, sound, connotation), while the sixth is about how many similar marks exist in the marketplace. How does the number of third-party marks change the 'commercial impression' of CC Serve's ASPIRE mark? Is the court saying that if there are many ASPIRE marks in financial services, consumers will perceive CC Serve's mark as weaker, and that weaker impression affects the first factor analysis? Is commercial strength part of the first factor, or is it exclusively a sixth factor consideration?

questions.title: How many third-party uses are needed to show a mark is 'weak' under the sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., the Board found that nine third-party ASPIRE-formative marks for credit card services did not rise to the level of 'considerable' or 'ubiquitous' use needed to demonstrate weakness. The court cited Jack Wolfskin (14 'notable examples' with 'voluminous evidence') and Juice Generation (26 marks as 'a considerable number'). Is there a minimum threshold number of third-party marks needed to establish weakness? Does the quality or notoriety of the third-party uses matter, or is it purely a numbers game? And if Apex introduces the additional 42 marks on remand, is there a number that would be dispositive, or does the Board still have discretion to weigh the evidence?

questions.title: What is a 'letter of protest' in trademark prosecution and how does it differ from a formal opposition?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., CC Serve submitted a 'letter of protest' to the USPTO during prosecution of Apex's applications, but the examining attorney still approved the marks for publication. CC Serve then filed a formal opposition. I'm confused about the procedural distinction. What is a letter of protest—who can submit one, what is the examining attorney's obligation to consider it, and what happens if it's ignored? How does it differ from an opposition proceeding before the TTAB? Is a letter of protest a prerequisite to filing an opposition, or could CC Serve have skipped it?

questions.title: What is the practical effect of 'affirm-in-part, vacate-in-part, and remand' on the trademark application?
questions.question_body: In Apex Bank v. CC Serve Corp., the court affirmed the second DuPont factor finding but vacated the first and sixth factor findings, remanding for the Board to reconsider. I'm trying to understand what happens procedurally. Does Apex's application remain suspended during remand? If the Board reconsiders factors 1 and 6 but reaches the same ultimate conclusion (likelihood of confusion exists), can Apex appeal again? Could the Board's reconsideration of the sixth factor lead to a finding that CC Serve's mark is weak enough that there's no likelihood of confusion, thus allowing Apex's registration? Also, the court awarded costs to appellant—does that mean Apex 'won' even though the Board's ultimate ruling was mostly affirmed?
